newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain strike impact wanes as negotiations resume.
newsitem.headline: Spain strike impact wanes as negotiations resume.

text.p: Spain's government resumed negotiations with striking truck drivers on Monday as the economic impact of the 12-day-old stoppage waned.
Commerce and traffic were returning to normal with security forces guaranteeing free movement on the roads, officials said.
"The country is totally normal," one government official told Reuters.
Some car-makers were forced to cut back or halt production on Monday for lack of parts but most effects on the economy were left over from last week's disruptions of traffic.
By Monday, civil guards had unblocked ports and main thoroughfares in northern Spain, the hardest hit region.

Under government orders to guarantee free circulation of traffic, security forces escorted any truckers who requested protection for fear of retaliation from strikers parked along the hard shoulders of roads.
Markets which had been emptied of produce by late last week were full again on Monday, the Agriculture Ministry said.

Taxi drivers had threatened to join the strike on Monday, demanding the same improvements in labour conditions and lower fuel prices which the truckers want. But only small demonstrations and partial stoppages were reported.
In Barcelona, drivers stopped work for six hours and blocked some roads.
In Madrid, about 200 taxis obstructed a main road to demonstrate in front of the Transport Ministry.
The truckers' organisation leading the strike, Fedatrans, was to resume negotiations with the government on Monday after lengthy sessions at the weekend failed to produce a solution.

Fedatrans was expected to submit a document to the government outlining their main disagreements and proposals to overcome them. Negotiations would resume in the afternoon after the government examined the proposal, officials said.
The key sticking point in the talks is the truckers' demand for early retirement -- at 60 instead of 65.
About 20 percent of Spain's truckers are between 60 and 65, according to truckers' associations.
Newspaper reports said some strikers who are not members of Fedatrans were abandoning the strike.

Nevertheless, Economy Secretary in the Catalan regional government Macia Alavedra warned on Monday the strike could ruin the government's efforts to reduce inflation which is one of the key criteria for entering a European Monetary Union in 1999.
Spanish inflation for January fell below 3.0 percent for the first time in 28 years.
Some car-makers in Spain and outside were reporting disruptions in production due to the strike.

German's Volkswagen AG said the elimination of two special weekend shifts had allowed it to maintain a normal production schedule for Monday despite a parts shortage at its Wolfsburg plant because of the Spanish strike.
A Volkswagen plant in Spain's Navarre region also stopped production on Monday for lack of supplies.
